# Public Evidence-Chain Report: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive Summary

The 2023 3CX DesktopApp compromise was a multi-stage software supply-chain operation in which attackers first compromised software associated with Trading Technologies, used that access to penetrate 3CX’s corporate environment, and then modified 3CX’s software build and distribution process. The resulting trojanized 3CX DesktopApp was distributed to a potentially very large customer base through legitimate, digitally signed installers.

The strongest public reconstruction comes from Mandiant’s investigation, published by Google Cloud. Mandiant identified a prior compromise of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software as the initial intrusion vector into 3CX. A 3CX employee installed the compromised X_TRADER package, allowing the attackers to establish a foothold, harvest credentials, move laterally, and compromise both Windows and macOS build environments. The attackers then inserted malicious components into the 3CX DesktopApp distribution chain. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The 3CX compromise affected versions of the Windows and macOS Electron applications. The malicious Windows application used a staged loader and downloader chain involving SUDDENICON, encrypted icon files hosted on GitHub, and ICONICSTEALER, a data-mining component capable of collecting browser information. A separate, more capable backdoor identified as Gopuram was deployed selectively against fewer than ten observed systems, with evidence indicating particular interest in cryptocurrency-related organizations. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Public attribution converged on a North Korea-linked threat cluster, but naming varied. Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, assessing with moderate confidence that it was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram deployment to **Lazarus** with medium to high confidence, while CrowdStrike-linked reporting associated the operation with **Labyrinth Chollima**, an identity associated with Lazarus in MITRE ATT&CK. These labels should not be treated as independently proven organizational identities; they represent different vendor naming and attribution frameworks applied to overlapping activity. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

The most defensible conclusion is that the 3CX compromise was conducted by a North Korea-linked, financially motivated cluster associated publicly with AppleJeus and Lazarus-related activity. The evidence is strong for the technical intrusion chain and moderate for the precise organizational attribution.

## Source and Evidence Registry

For clarity, the sources provided in the evidence set are assigned the following source IDs:

| Source ID | Source | Principal evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Cybersecurity Dive, March 30, 2023 | Early reporting on affected versions, scale, initial detections, and suspected Labyrinth Chollima involvement |
| S2 | WIRED, April 3, 2023 | Evidence concerning selective targeting of cryptocurrency firms and Gopuram deployment |
| S3 | Mandiant/Google Cloud, April 20, 2023 | Detailed reconstruction of the initial Trading Technologies compromise, 3CX intrusion, build-environment compromise, malware chain, and attribution |
| S4 | Kaspersky Securelist, April 3, 2023 | Analysis of Gopuram, selective targeting, cryptocurrency focus, and Lazarus attribution |
| S5 | Google Threat Analysis Group, March 24, 2022 | Earlier AppleJeus activity, Trading Technologies compromise, and North Korea-linked cryptocurrency targeting |
| S6 | MITRE ATT&CK AppleJeus profile | AppleJeus relationships, capabilities, and association with Lazarus |
| S7 | MITRE ATT&CK Lazarus Group profile | Lazarus aliases, attribution caveats, and relevant tradecraft |
| S8 | Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, March 31, 2023 | Public advisory identifying affected Windows and macOS application versions and recommended response |

## Scope and Method

This report reconstructs only the public evidence chain contained in the supplied sources. It distinguishes between:

1. **Observed or reconstructed technical facts**, such as malware components, file paths, and build-environment activity;
2. **Vendor assessments**, such as Mandiant’s assessment that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity; and
3. **Media or researcher characterizations**, such as descriptions of the campaign as a Lazarus operation or a cryptocurrency-focused theft campaign.

The report does not treat the number of potentially exposed customers as equivalent to the number of confirmed compromised organizations. Several sources describe a large distribution footprint, but the available evidence indicates that the attackers selectively deployed later-stage tooling to a much smaller subset of victims.

## Initial Compromise: The Trading Technologies Supply-Chain Attack

### X_TRADER as the initial intrusion vector

Mandiant reported that the initial compromise of 3CX’s network occurred through malicious software downloaded from the Trading Technologies website. Specifically, Mandiant identified a tampered installer for **X_TRADER**, a Trading Technologies software package that remained available for download even though the platform had reportedly been discontinued. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The identified installer was named:

`X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe`

Mandiant reported the MD5 hash:

`ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`

The installer and its embedded `Setup.exe` were digitally signed with a certificate associated with “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” Mandiant stated that the certificate was due to expire in October 2022. The presence of a valid or apparently legitimate signature helped the malicious package appear trustworthy. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The X_TRADER installer deployed a modular backdoor identified by Mandiant as **VEILEDSIGNAL**. The infection process relied on two malicious DLLs and a benign executable. The benign executable was used to side-load a malicious DLL, after which the attackers used the SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL components to decrypt and load the payload into memory. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### How the earlier compromise reached 3CX

According to Mandiant, a 3CX employee installed the compromised X_TRADER software. This provided the attackers with access to a 3CX endpoint and, subsequently, the 3CX corporate environment. Mandiant’s account is significant because it links the two supply-chain compromises directly rather than merely identifying similarities between them. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The sequence reconstructed from the public evidence is:

1. Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER installer was compromised.
2. The compromised installer was distributed from the legitimate Trading Technologies website.
3. A 3CX employee installed the compromised package.
4. The attackers used the resulting access to enter the 3CX environment.
5. The attackers harvested credentials and moved laterally.
6. The attackers compromised the 3CX Windows and macOS build environments.
7. Malicious code was inserted into 3CX DesktopApp installers.
8. Tro­janized installers were distributed to 3CX customers.

This is the central finding of the case. Mandiant described it as the first confirmed instance known to the company in which one software supply-chain attack directly enabled another software supply-chain attack. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

## Propagation Through the 3CX Build Environment

### Credential harvesting and lateral movement

After gaining access to the 3CX environment, the attackers harvested credentials and moved laterally. Mandiant reported that the adversary used a compiled version of the open-source **Fast Reverse Proxy** project during internal movement. A file named `MsMpEng.exe`, with MD5 hash `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, was placed in `C:\Windows\System32`. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The use of a filename resembling a Microsoft security component is consistent with masquerading, although the supplied evidence does not establish every execution detail associated with that file. Mandiant’s account does establish that the attackers moved through the 3CX environment and reached development infrastructure.

### Compromise of Windows and macOS build servers

Mandiant reported that the attackers ultimately compromised both the Windows and macOS build environments used by 3CX. On the Windows build environment, they deployed:

- **TAXHAUL**, a launcher;
- **COLDCAT**, a downloader; and
- persistence through DLL search-order hijacking involving the IKEEXT service.

The malicious components operated with LocalSystem privileges, according to Mandiant. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The macOS build server was compromised with **POOLRAT**, which used Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant clarified that a sample previously described as a potentially separate macOS backdoor, SIMPLESEA, was determined through further analysis to be POOLRAT. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

This build-environment compromise was the decisive stage in the propagation process. The attackers were no longer limited to individual 3CX systems. They had access to the systems responsible for producing or packaging software intended for 3CX’s customers.

## Trojanization and Distribution of 3CX DesktopApp

### Affected versions and platforms

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore reported that the trojanized application affected the following versions:

| Platform | Affected versions |
|---|---|
| Windows Electron application | 18.12.407 and 18.12.416 |
| macOS Electron application | 18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416 |

The advisory stated that the malware could harvest system information and steal data and stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles. ([S8](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

The early reporting described the application as widely deployed, with 3CX claiming more than 600,000 corporate customers and more than 12 million active daily users. Huntress also reported more than 242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems based on Shodan data, although public exposure of a management system should not be equated with confirmed infection. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

### Technical infection chain

Mandiant described the malicious Windows 3CX application as containing code that launched a downloader called **SUDDENICON**. SUDDENICON retrieved additional command-and-control information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. The decrypted infrastructure was then used to download **ICONICSTEALER**, a data-mining component that collected browser information. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Kaspersky similarly reported that the malicious installer contained an infected DLL that decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`. The resulting payload extracted command-and-control server URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository. The downloaded infostealer collected system information and browser history. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

The use of GitHub in this chain did not mean that GitHub itself was the original compromise vector. The public evidence describes GitHub as a hosting or retrieval mechanism used by the malware after the trojanized 3CX application had executed.

### Signed software and DLL side-loading

Early reporting from Cybersecurity Dive stated that CrowdStrike observed malicious activity from a legitimate, signed binary. Sophos researchers described the attack as involving DLL side-loading, which enabled malicious code to execute within the context of a trusted application. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

This combination—legitimate software distribution, valid signing, DLL side-loading, and staged payload retrieval—helped the attackers reach a large number of systems while delaying detection. The Singapore advisory accordingly recommended uninstalling affected versions, conducting full antivirus scans, and blocking known malicious domains and indicators. ([S8](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

## Selective Follow-On Targeting and Gopuram

### Broad exposure versus narrow exploitation

Although the compromised 3CX application was distributed broadly, the available evidence indicates that the most capable follow-on backdoor was deployed selectively. Kaspersky reported that Gopuram was observed on fewer than ten infected machines in its telemetry. It also reported that the observed victims included cryptocurrency companies and that the attackers appeared to select targets with “surgical precision.” ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

WIRED reported the same general distinction: a potentially massive supply-chain compromise was used to identify and filter victims, after which the attackers focused on a small number of cryptocurrency-related organizations. ([S2](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/))

This supports a two-level operational model:

- **First stage:** broad distribution of a reconnaissance and information-stealing component;
- **Second stage:** selective deployment of a full backdoor against high-value targets.

The evidence does not prove that every victim was a cryptocurrency organization, nor does it establish that cryptocurrency theft was successfully completed. Kaspersky specifically stated that it had not observed evidence of actual cryptocurrency theft from the Gopuram-infected organizations within its telemetry. ([S2](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/))

### Gopuram capabilities

Kaspersky identified **Gopuram** as a modular backdoor that could interact with the victim’s file system and create processes. It observed the following related components and functions:

| Component or module | Reported function |
|---|---|
| `wlbsctrl.dll` | Decrypts and executes shellcode |
| `guard64.dll` | Main Gopuram backdoor module |
| `Ping` | Pings a specified host |
| `Connect` | Establishes a socket connection |
| `Registry` | Lists, adds, deletes, and exports registry keys |
| `Service` | Creates, lists, starts, stops, and deletes services |
| `Timestomp` | Alters file timestamps |
| `Inject` | Performs payload injection |
| `KDU` | Loads an unsigned driver and gathers security-product information |
| `Update` | Encrypts and stores a payload in the TxR directory |
| `Net` | Performs selected user, group, session, and share-management functions |

Kaspersky reported that `wlbsctrl.dll` was loaded by the IKEEXT service through DLL hijacking and decrypted an encrypted shellcode payload stored under:

`C:\Windows\System32\config\TxR\<machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms`

It also reported the path `C:\Windows\system32\catroot2\edb.chk.log` as associated with the tooling. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

## Public Attribution

### Mandiant’s UNC4736 assessment

Mandiant tracked the 3CX activity as **UNC4736**, describing it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. The assessment was based on malware, infrastructure, and tradecraft overlaps, including POOLRAT, CoinGoTrade, JMT Trading, and infrastructure associated with cryptocurrency targeting. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Mandiant also identified similarities between the compromised X_TRADER and 3CX applications, including:

- the same RC4 key, `3jB(2bsG#@c7`;
- use of SIGFLIP;
- use of DAVESHELL;
- the hard-coded cookie variable `__tutma`; and
- AES-256-GCM encryption.

These overlaps support common tooling or operator continuity, but they do not independently prove the legal identity of the attacker. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Kaspersky’s Lazarus assessment

Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram activity to Lazarus with medium to high confidence. Its reasoning included the coexistence of Gopuram and AppleJeus on a previously investigated cryptocurrency-company network, infrastructure overlap with AppleJeus operations, and domains previously associated by researchers with Lazarus. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

MITRE ATT&CK identifies AppleJeus as malware used by Lazarus Group and describes AppleJeus as a family of downloaders originally embedded in trojanized cryptocurrency applications. MITRE also identifies Lazarus as a North Korean state-sponsored group associated with the Reconnaissance General Bureau, while cautioning that public reporting often uses “Lazarus Group” as an umbrella term for multiple North Korean operators. ([S6](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/); [S7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

### Labyrinth Chollima and other names

Early CrowdStrike-linked reporting associated the activity with **Labyrinth Chollima**, a North Korea-linked group. MITRE lists Labyrinth Chollima among the associated names for Lazarus Group. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

However, the supplied WIRED article describing the later Mandiant findings used other labels, including Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima. That naming differs from Mandiant’s UNC4736 designation and from Kaspersky’s Lazarus assessment. The discrepancy demonstrates the attribution uncertainty surrounding North Korean cyber operations, where vendors may track related activity under different cluster names. ([S9](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two/))

## Contradictions and Uncertainties

### Contradiction 1: Attribution labels

Early reporting associated the activity with Labyrinth Chollima, Mandiant used UNC4736, Kaspersky assessed Lazarus involvement, and one WIRED article used Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima. These labels are not fully consistent. The most cautious interpretation is that the campaign was North Korea-linked and related to AppleJeus/Lazarus-associated activity, while the exact sub-group identity remains uncertain. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S9](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two/))

### Contradiction 2: Scope of macOS confirmation

Cybersecurity Dive reported that CrowdStrike observed activity on Windows and macOS, while noting that other researchers had not confirmed macOS activity. Kaspersky stated that an installer for macOS had also been trojanized, and Mandiant reported compromise of the macOS build server with POOLRAT. These statements concern different levels of the chain—customer-side execution versus build-server compromise—and therefore should not automatically be treated as mutually exclusive. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

### Uncertainty about ultimate objectives

The cryptocurrency focus is well supported by victimology, Gopuram history, AppleJeus associations, and Trading Technologies-related infrastructure. Nevertheless, the sources do not establish the full operational objective or prove successful cryptocurrency theft. The evidence supports a financially motivated hypothesis, not a definitive account of all attacker goals. ([S2](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/); [S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

## Findings

### Finding 1: How was the 3CX compromise initiated?

The strongest public evidence indicates that the 3CX compromise was initiated through a prior compromise of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software. A 3CX employee installed the tampered software, which provided attackers with access to the 3CX environment. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Finding 2: How did the compromise propagate?

The attackers used access obtained through the compromised X_TRADER installation to harvest credentials, move laterally within 3CX, compromise Windows and macOS build environments, and insert malicious code into 3CX DesktopApp installers. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Finding 3: What was distributed to customers?

Trojanized Windows and macOS Electron application versions were distributed through the legitimate 3CX software channel. The Windows chain involved SUDDENICON, GitHub-hosted encrypted icon files, and ICONICSTEALER. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S8](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

### Finding 4: Was the entire customer base fully compromised?

No. The application distribution created broad exposure, but Gopuram was observed on fewer than ten systems in Kaspersky’s telemetry. This indicates selective follow-on targeting rather than uniform deployment of the final backdoor. ([S2](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

### Finding 5: Which activity cluster was the campaign attributed to?

The campaign was publicly attributed to a North Korea-linked cluster. Mandiant tracked it as UNC4736 and assessed a moderate-confidence relationship to financially motivated AppleJeus activity; Kaspersky assessed Lazarus involvement with medium to high confidence; early reporting used Labyrinth Chollima. The precise sub-group attribution remains uncertain, but Lazarus/AppleJeus-related North Korean activity is the most consistent public attribution. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S6](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/); [S7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

## Conclusion

The public evidence supports a clear cascading supply-chain model. The attackers did not initially compromise 3CX through a direct attack on its software distribution infrastructure. Instead, they first compromised Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software. That compromised package was installed by a 3CX employee, giving the attackers an entry point into 3CX. They then harvested credentials, moved laterally, compromised build servers, and inserted malicious code into the 3CX DesktopApp production and distribution chain.

The resulting customer-side malware was staged and modular. The broad first-stage deployment enabled reconnaissance and information theft, while Gopuram was reserved for a small number of selectively chosen systems. The available victimology and malware relationships indicate a strong interest in cryptocurrency and fintech organizations.

My assessment is that the technical propagation chain is established with high confidence from Mandiant’s investigation. The North Korea-linked attribution is also well supported by overlapping malware, infrastructure, and targeting patterns. However, the exact internal identity of the responsible operator should remain expressed as **UNC4736 / AppleJeus-related North Korean activity, publicly associated with Lazarus and Labyrinth Chollima**, rather than as an unqualified assertion that one specific named group definitively conducted every stage.
